summary.text: At the prime-power level, define \(\mu_0=0\), \(\mu_{2m+1}=2^{2m+1}\), and \(\mu_{2m}=4^m(2\mu_m-1)\); induction gives \(\mu_m\ge0\), so the recurrence \(c_0=1\), \(c_n=(2n)^{-1}\sum_{j<n}\mu_{n-j}c_j\) gives \(c_n\ge0\), while logarithmic-derivative identities show \(c*c\) has coefficients \(2^{\sum_k\lfloor n/2^k\rfloor}\). Extending \(c\) multiplicatively therefore yields the required Dirichlet square root, whose value at each integer is \(\prod_p c_{v_p(n)}\) and is consequently nonnegative.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(e)=\sum_{k\ge 0}\left\lfloor\frac e{2^k}\right\rfloor.
\]
Only finitely many summands are nonzero, so this agrees with the definition of A005187 used in A046644. Define the multiplicative arithmetic function
\[
A(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}2^{S(e)}\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
Thus \(A=A046644\). We shall construct a multiplicative arithmetic function \(F\), nonnegative at every positive integer, such that
\[
F*F=A,
\]
where \(*\) denotes Dirichlet convolution. We will then prove that \(F\) is exactly the recursively specified square root \(A317940_f\).

The main part of the argument is the construction of the values of \(F\) on prime powers.

### 1. Two auxiliary exponent sequences

Define rational sequences \((a_e)_{e\ge0}\) and \((\mu_e)_{e\ge0}\) recursively as follows:
\[
a_0=1,
\]
and, for \(m\ge0\),
\[
a_{2m}=4^m a_m,
\qquad
 a_{2m+1}=2\cdot4^m a_m.
\]
(The even formula also gives \(a_0=a_0\), but we take \(a_0=1\) as the initial condition.) Define
\[
\mu_0=0,
\]
and
\[
\mu_{2m+1}=2^{2m+1}\qquad(m\ge0),
\]
while for \(m\ge1\),
\[
\mu_{2m}=4^m(2\mu_m-1).
\]
These recurrences are well founded because each positive index is reduced to roughly half its size.

We first note that
\[
\mu_e\ge0\quad\text{for every }e,
\]
and in fact
\[
\mu_e\ge1\quad\text{for every }e\ge1.
\]
This follows by strong induction on \(e\). If \(e=2m+1\), then
\(\mu_e=2^e\ge1\). If \(e=2m\ge2\), then \(m\ge1\), so the induction hypothesis gives \(\mu_m\ge1\). Hence
\[
2\mu_m-1\ge1,
\]
and therefore
\[
\mu_e=4^m(2\mu_m-1)\ge1.
\]
Together with \(\mu_0=0\), this proves the assertion.

We next identify \(a_e\). The floor sum satisfies
\[
S(2m)=2m+S(m)\qquad(m\ge1)
\]
and
\[
S(2m+1)=2m+1+S(m)\qquad(m\ge0).
\]
Indeed, the term with \(k=0\) is the number itself, and for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2m}{2^{k+1}}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac m{2^k}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{2m+1}{2^{k+1}}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac m{2^k}\right\rfloor.
\]
There is no issue in shifting or truncating the sums: for \(j\ge m\), one has \(m<2^m\le2^j\), so \(\lfloor m/2^j\rfloor=0\).

It now follows by strong induction that
\[
 a_e=2^{S(e)}\qquad(e\ge0).
\]
For \(e=0\), both sides are 1. If \(e=2m\ge2\), then
\[
a_{2m}=4^m a_m
       =2^{2m}2^{S(m)}
       =2^{S(2m)}.
\]
If \(e=2m+1\), then
\[
a_{2m+1}=2\cdot4^m a_m
         =2^{2m+1}2^{S(m)}
         =2^{S(2m+1)}.
\]
Thus \(a_e\) is precisely the desired local value of A046644 at a prime power of exponent \(e\).

### 2. A logarithmic-derivative identity for \(a_e\)

For \(N\ge0\), put
\[
T_N=\sum_{j=0}^N\mu_j a_{N-j}.
\]
We prove the key identity
\[
\boxed{\quad T_N=N a_N\quad}                                      \tag{1}
\]
for every \(N\ge0\).

Since \(\mu_0=0\), we can also write
\[
T_N=\sum_{r=1}^N\mu_r a_{N-r}.
\]
We first derive recurrences for \(T_N\) by pairing its even- and odd-indexed terms.

For \(N\ge0\),
\[
T_{2N}=2\,4^N T_N.                                                  \tag{2}
\]
To see this, omit the zero term indexed by 0 and pair, for each \(0\le i<N\), the terms indexed by \(2(i+1)\) and \(2i+1\). Put
\[
k=N-i-1,
\]
so that \(i+1+k=N\). The paired terms are
\[
\mu_{2(i+1)}a_{2N-2(i+1)}+
\mu_{2i+1}a_{2N-(2i+1)}.
\]
Using the recurrences for \(a\) and \(\mu\), this equals
\[
4^{i+1}(2\mu_{i+1}-1)\,4^k a_k
 +2^{2i+1}\,2\,4^k a_k.
\]
Because \(2^{2i+1}\cdot2=4^{i+1}\), the two terms combine to
\[
2\,4^{i+1+k}\mu_{i+1}a_k
 =2\,4^N\mu_{i+1}a_{N-(i+1)}.
\]
Summing over \(i=0,\ldots,N-1\) gives (2).

Likewise,
\[
T_{2N+1}=2\,4^N a_N+4^{N+1}T_N.                                   \tag{3}
\]
For this sum, the term indexed by 0 again vanishes. The term indexed by 1 is
\[
\mu_1a_{2N}=2\,4^N a_N.
\]
The remaining terms can be paired, for \(0\le i<N\), using indices \(2(i+1)\) and \(2(i+1)+1\). Again set \(k=N-i-1\). Their sum is
\[
\mu_{2(i+1)}a_{2k+1}+
\mu_{2(i+1)+1}a_{2k}.
\]
Substitution gives
\[
4^{i+1}(2\mu_{i+1}-1)\,2\,4^k a_k
 +2^{2(i+1)+1}\,4^k a_k.
\]
Since \(2^{2(i+1)+1}=2\,4^{i+1}\), this becomes
\[
4\,4^N\mu_{i+1}a_k.
\]
Summing these paired terms produces \(4\,4^N T_N=4^{N+1}T_N\), proving (3).

We can now prove (1) by strong induction. It is immediate for \(N=0\), since \(T_0=\mu_0a_0=0\). Suppose first that the index is \(2N>0\). By (2), the induction hypothesis, and the recurrence for \(a\),
\[
T_{2N}=2\,4^N T_N
      =2\,4^N(Na_N)
      =(2N)(4^N a_N)
      =(2N)a_{2N}.
\]
For an odd index, (3) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{2N+1}
 &=2\,4^N a_N+4^{N+1}(Na_N)\\
 &=2(2N+1)4^N a_N\\
 &=(2N+1)a_{2N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This completes the proof of (1).

### 3. Construction and nonnegativity of the local square root

Define rational numbers \(c_n\) recursively by
\[
c_0=1
\]
and, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
\boxed{\quad
c_n=\frac1{2n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mu_{n-j}c_j.
\quad}                                                             \tag{4}
\]
This uniquely defines \(c_n\), because only earlier values \(c_j\), with \(j<n\), occur on the right.

Every \(c_n\) is nonnegative. This is another strong induction. The base value is \(c_0=1\). For \(n\ge1\), the factor \(1/(2n)\) is positive, every \(\mu_{n-j}\) is nonnegative, and every \(c_j\) appearing in the sum is nonnegative by induction. Thus every summand in (4) is nonnegative, hence \(c_n\ge0\).

Reversing the order of summation in (4), and using \(\mu_0=0\), gives the equivalent convolution identity
\[
\boxed{\quad
\sum_{j=0}^n\mu_jc_{n-j}=2n c_n.
\quad}                                                             \tag{5}
\]
For \(n=0\), both sides are zero, so (5) holds for all \(n\ge0\).

We next prove that \(c\) is a convolution square root of \(a\) in the exponent variable:
\[
\boxed{\quad
\sum_{j=0}^n c_jc_{n-j}=a_n
\quad}                                                             \tag{6}
\]
for every \(n\ge0\).

Introduce formal power series over \(\mathbb Q\):
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n,
\qquad
M(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}\mu_nx^n,
\qquad
C(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nx^n.
\]
For a series \(P(x)=\sum p_nx^n\), let
\[
D(P)=xP'(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}n p_nx^n.
\]
Identity (1) says coefficientwise that
\[
D(A)=MA.                                                           \tag{7}
\]
Identity (5) similarly says
\[
MC=2D(C).                                                          \tag{8}
\]

Let \(Q=C^2\). We claim
\[
D(Q)=MQ.                                                           \tag{9}
\]
This follows directly either from the formal product rule or coefficientwise. Indeed,
\[
D(C^2)=2C\,D(C)=C(MC)=M C^2,
\]
where (8) was used in the middle equality.

For completeness, the coefficient calculation behind the product rule is as follows. If
\[
q_n=\sum_{j=0}^n c_jc_{n-j},
\]
then
\[
nq_n=\sum_{j=0}^n n c_jc_{n-j}.
\]
Writing \(n=j+(n-j)\), the symmetry under \(j\leftrightarrow n-j\) shows that this is
\[
2\sum_{j=0}^n j c_jc_{n-j}.
\]
Using (5), \(2j c_j=\sum_{r=0}^j\mu_r c_{j-r}\), and regrouping the resulting finite sums gives precisely the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(MC^2\). Thus (9) is an entirely coefficientwise formal identity.

Both \(A\) and \(Q=C^2\) have constant coefficient 1: \(a_0=1\), while the constant coefficient of \(C^2\) is \(c_0^2=1\). Equations (7) and (9) now force \(Q=A\). Here is the coefficient induction establishing uniqueness. Suppose the coefficients of \(Q\) and \(A\) agree below degree \(n\), where \(n>0\). Because \(\mu_0=0\), the coefficient of degree \(n\) in \(M Q\) is
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n\mu_j q_{n-j},
\]
and depends only on coefficients of \(Q\) below degree \(n\). By the induction hypothesis it therefore equals the degree-\(n\) coefficient of \(MA\). From (7) and (9),
\[
nq_n=[x^n](MQ)=[x^n](MA)=n a_n.
\]
Since \(n\ne0\) in \(\mathbb Q\), cancellation gives \(q_n=a_n\). Starting from the common constant coefficient, induction proves \(C^2=A\), which is exactly (6).

### 4. Lifting the local square root to arithmetic functions

Define, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
F(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}c_e.
\]
Also define
\[
\widetilde A(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}2^{S(e)}
               =\prod_{p^e\parallel n}a_e.
\]
Both functions are multiplicative: if \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime, their sets of prime divisors are disjoint, and the prime factorization of \(mn\) is obtained by adjoining the two factorizations. The empty product gives
\[
F(1)=\widetilde A(1)=1.
\]
Moreover, for every prime \(p\) and \(i\ge0\),
\[
F(p^i)=c_i,
\qquad
\widetilde A(p^i)=2^{S(i)}=a_i.
\]

The Dirichlet convolution of multiplicative functions is multiplicative. Hence \(F*F\) and \(\widetilde A\) are both multiplicative, so it is enough to compare them on prime powers. The divisors of \(p^i\) are \(p^j\), \(0\le j\le i\), and therefore (6) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
(F*F)(p^i)
 &=\sum_{j=0}^i F(p^j)F(p^{i-j})\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^i c_jc_{i-j}\\
 &=a_i\\
 &=\widetilde A(p^i).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
F*F=\widetilde A.
\]
But by its defining prime-factor product, \(\widetilde A\) is exactly A046644. Consequently,
\[
\boxed{\quad F*F=A046644.\quad}                                   \tag{10}
\]

Also, since every local factor \(c_e\) is nonnegative,
\[
F(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}c_e\ge0                                \tag{11}
\]
for every \(n\ge1\).

### 5. Identification with the recursively defined sequence

It remains to check that this nonnegative square root is the particular square root \(f=A317940_f\) used in the definition of A317940.

That sequence is specified by
\[
f(1)=1
\]
and, for \(n\ge2\),
\[
f(n)=\frac12\left(A046644(n)-
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}f(d)f(n/d)\right).               \tag{12}
\]
This recursion is well founded: if \(1<d<n\) and \(d\mid n\), then both \(d<n\) and \(n/d<n\).

We show by strong induction on \(n\) that
\[
F(n)=f(n).
\]
At \(n=1\), both values are 1. (If the auxiliary value at 0 is included, both definitions assign 0 there as well.) Now let \(n\ge2\), and suppose equality has already been proved at every smaller positive integer.

Splitting the divisor sum in (10) into the endpoint divisors \(1,n\) and the proper divisors gives
\[
A046644(n)
 =(F*F)(n)
 =F(1)F(n)+F(n)F(1)
   +\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}F(d)F(n/d).
\]
Since \(F(1)=1\), this is
\[
A046644(n)
 =2F(n)+\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}F(d)F(n/d).              \tag{13}
\]
For every divisor in the remaining sum, both arguments \(d\) and \(n/d\) are smaller than \(n\), so the induction hypothesis replaces both occurrences of \(F\) by \(f\). Solving (13) for \(F(n)\) then gives
\[
F(n)=\frac12\left(A046644(n)-
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}f(d)f(n/d)\right)=f(n)
\]
by (12). This completes the induction.

Combining this identification with (11), for every \(n\ge1\) we obtain
\[
A317940_f(n)=f(n)=F(n)\ge0.
\]
Therefore the rational Dirichlet-convolution square root underlying A317940 is nonnegative at every positive integer. Since a rational number in reduced form has positive denominator, its numerator has the same sign; hence the numerators forming OEIS A317940 are nonnegative as claimed.
